public_code_and_technical_footprint:
### Disclosed AI and application stack

ChanceRAG provides the clearest technical disclosure. Rabbitt says it fuses vector retrieval with BM25 keyword retrieval, uses Mistral embeddings, and uses Annoy for approximate-nearest-neighbor retrieval. [public_code_and_technical_footprint[0]] [28] This is a conventional hybrid-RAG architecture with a specific embedding and vector-search implementation. The public page does not provide reproducible benchmarks, an open repository, infrastructure topology, data-retention controls, or evidence for any patent status.

DRIP discloses application-level components rather than backend architecture: a Monaco-based browser IDE, execution results, complexity analysis, test validation, an AI mentor, AI interviewers, recorded sessions, dashboards, integrations with HR/learning systems, and agent challenges. [public_code_and_technical_footprint[1]] [9] Publicly served markup on the DRIP, Rabbitt Learning, and Code Bunny sites contains Next.js-style `/_next/static` assets; this is a frontend OSINT inference, not proof of the backend, database, cloud, or model-serving stack.

[public_code_and_technical_footprint[3]] [26] | MIT-licensed but extremely early: created July 25, 2024, one commit, one star, zero forks, and an explicit warning about broken or unimplemented features. [public_code_and_technical_footprint[4]] [25] | Sparse experimental repository. No public license or release was exposed. Its relationship to the separately cased `RabbittAi` user is not explained. |

The code footprint does not demonstrate the production implementation of ChanceRAG, DRIP, Code Bunny, or customer deployments. Bunny's README ambition - an open-source alternative to autonomous software-engineering systems - aligns with Rabbitt's 2024 statement that it was creating a GenAI autonomous software engineer, but the repository itself labels the work experimental.
